content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a values framework to guide the allocation and prioritization of COVID-19 vaccination. This framework is accessible online and was last reviewed on May 31, 2023. 2. WHO has also provided methods for assessing influenza vaccination coverage in target groups, which can be applied to pandemic planning. These methods were last accessed on May 31, 2023. 3. The objectives of pandemic vaccination planning include outlining strategies and key considerations for delivering vaccines against influenza or other respiratory illnesses to priority populations, such as school-going children, working adults, older populations, healthcare workers, and the general public. 4. Lessons learned from previous adult vaccination programs, such as those for seasonal influenza, hepatitis B (in healthcare workers), measles, rubella, and Japanese encephalitis, can inform pandemic vaccination planning. These lessons are particularly useful for determining the location and timing of vaccination sessions, as well as for planning human resources and training. 5. Countries are encouraged to engage with communities through surveys, focus group discussions, opinion polls, and open meetings to increase vaccine acceptance and maximize uptake. Public engagement activities help understand attitudes toward vaccination, including preferences for timing, delivery strategies, and public versus private sector involvement. 6. Vaccine delivery strategies should consider cost implications, such as whether vaccines will be provided free of charge to all, only to specific populations like healthcare workers and low-income groups, or at a subsidized cost. 7. WHO will provide recommended immunization schedules for approved pandemic vaccines based on clinical trial findings and advice from the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE). These recommendations will be available during the pandemic. 8. If multiple vaccine types are available, as seen during the COVID-19 pandemic, national immunization technical advisory groups (NITAGs) should review and recommend their interchangeability based on WHO SAGE guidance and scientific evidence. 9. Pandemic vaccination schedules should account for the specific needs of medically vulnerable groups, such as individuals with prior infection, immunocompromised persons, pregnant women, and breastfeeding mothers. 10. Countries should identify a mix of vaccine delivery options, including fixed sites, mobile clinics, and outreach strategies, to maximize vaccination coverage. Examples include community care centers, pharmacies, marketplaces, parks, stadiums, and drive-through sites. 11. Vaccination strategies should address the needs of disadvantaged groups, such as older populations, individuals with underlying medical conditions, and internally displaced persons, who may lack access to fixed vaccination sites. 12. Mobile clinics and vans can be used to reach dispersed populations in remote areas, migrants, nomads, and workers in occupations like construction or agriculture. 13. Comprehensive micro-plans should be developed to ensure optimal resource utilization, including the size of target populations, the number of trained vaccinators, and vaccine dose requirements, while accounting for potential wastage. 14. Vaccination session sites should be well-ventilated and provide adequate physical distancing. They should include designated areas for waiting, vaccination, and observation, with provisions for accessibility and privacy. 15. Eligible beneficiaries should be reminded of their vaccination appointments through home visits, phone calls, or automated text messages. Follow-up efforts should be made for those who miss their appointments, leveraging local influencers or vaccine champions. 16. Vaccination teams must be equipped to manage adverse events following immunization (AEFIs), particularly anaphylaxis. Emergency transport should be available for beneficiaries requiring follow-up care. 17. Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are critical at vaccination sites to prevent the spread of the pandemic disease. This includes ensuring the availability of personal protective equipment (PPE) in various sizes and training health workers on IPC protocols. 18. Countries should integrate pandemic vaccination efforts with other health interventions, such as routine immunization, to optimize the use of human and financial resources. For example, vaccination of high-risk groups like pregnant women can be conducted through antenatal clinics or specialist clinics for chronic conditions. 19. Supply chain planning should include provisions for vaccine storage, transportation, and tracking. This involves estimating vaccine doses, cold chain requirements, and medical waste disposal needs. 20. Trained human resources are essential for supply chain management, including cold chain maintenance, vaccine packaging, stock monitoring, and emergency response planning. 21. Countries should conduct simulation exercises to assess the readiness of their systems for emergency vaccine deployment. 22. Most countries will rely on international shipments for pandemic vaccines, making global supply chains a critical factor. Planning should account for vaccine stability during transport, especially in remote areas requiring alternative modes of transportation like boats or drones.
